cues.en: Ladies and gentlemen, it's my privilege to introduce the messenger lecturer, Professor Richard P. Feynman of the California Institute of Technology. Professor Feynman is a distinguished theoretical physicist, and he's done much to bring order out of the confusion, which has marked much of the spectacular development in physics during the post-war period. Among his honors and awards, I will mention only the Albert Einstein Award in 1954.
cues.zh: 女士们、先生们，我很荣幸向大家介绍今晚信使系列讲座的主讲人，来自 California Institute of Technology 的 Richard P. Feynman 教授。Feynman 教授是一位杰出的理论物理学家，二战后物理学经历了突飞猛进的发展，但也伴随着诸多混乱，而他在拨云见日、理清头绪方面做出了巨大贡献。在他获得的众多荣誉和奖项中，我只提一下 1954 年的 Albert Einstein Award。

cues.en: This is an award which is made every third year and which includes a gold medal and a substantial sum of money. Professor Feynman did his undergraduate work at MIT and his graduate work at Princeton. He worked on the Manhattan Project at Princeton and later at Los Alamos. He was appointed an assistant professor here at Cornell in 1944, although he did not assume residence until the end of the war.
cues.zh: 该奖项每三年颁发一次，包括一枚金质奖章和一笔丰厚的奖金。Feynman 教授在 MIT 完成了本科学业，在 Princeton 获得了研究生学位。他曾在 Princeton 以及后来的 Los Alamos 参与了 Manhattan Project。他于 1944 年被任命为 Cornell 的助理教授，不过直到二战结束后他才正式到校任职。

cues.en: I thought it might be interesting to see what was said about him when he was appointed at Cornell, so I searched the minutes of our Board of Trustees, and there's absolutely no record of his appointment. There are, however, some 20 references to leaves of absence, salary, and promotions. One reference interested me especially.
cues.zh: 我想看看他当年在 Cornell 获聘时大家是怎么评价他的，这应该挺有意思，于是我查阅了校董事会的会议记录，结果居然完全没有关于他聘任的记录。不过，倒是大约有 20 处提到了他的请假、薪水和晋升。其中有一条记录让我格外感兴趣。

cues.en: On July 31, 1945, the chairman of the physics department wrote the dean of the arts college stating that Dr. Feynman is an outstanding teacher and investigator, the equal of whom develops infrequently. The chairman suggested that an annual salary of $3,000 was a bit too low for a distinguished faculty member.
cues.zh: 1945 年 7 月 31 日，物理系系主任写信给文理学院院长，称 Feynman 博士是一位杰出的教师和研究者，像他这样的人才极为罕见。系主任提出，对于一位如此卓越的教职员工来说，3000 美元的年薪实在有些偏低，

cues.en: and recommended that Professor Feynman's salary be increased $900. The dean, in an act of unusual generosity and with complete disregard for the solvency of the university, crossed out the $900 and made it an even thousand. You can see that we thought highly of Professor Feynman even then.
cues.zh: 并建议给 Feynman 教授加薪 900 美元。院长则表现出了异乎寻常的慷慨，完全不顾学校的财政承受能力，直接划掉了 900 美元，凑了个整，加了 1000 美元。由此可见，即便在那个时候，我们就已经对 Feynman 教授评价极高了。

cues.en: Feynman took up residence here at the end of 1945 and spent five highly productive years on our faculty. He left Cornell in 1950 and went to Caltech where he has been ever since. Before I let him talk, I want to tell you just a little bit more about him. Three or four years ago, he started teaching a beginning physics course at Caltech, and the result has added a new dimension to his fame. His lectures are now published in two volumes.
cues.zh: Feynman 于 1945 年底来到这里定居任教，在我们的师资队伍中度过了成果极其丰硕的五年。他于 1950 年离开 Cornell 前往 Caltech，并在那里一直工作至今。在请他开讲之前，我还想向大家多介绍一点关于他的事。三四年前，他在 Caltech 开设了一门基础物理课程，这门课让他的声誉又达到了一个新的高度。他的讲义现已整理成两卷出版，

cues.en: and they represent a refreshing approach to the subject. In the preface of the published lectures, there's a picture of Feynman performing happily on the bongo drums. My Caltech friends tell me that he sometimes drops in on the Los Angeles night spots and takes over the work of the drummer, but Professor Feynman tells me that that's not so. Another of his specialties is safe cracking.
cues.zh: 展现了一种令人耳目一新的教学视角。在已出版的讲义序言中，有一张 Feynman 欢快地演奏邦戈鼓的照片。我在 Caltech 的朋友告诉我，他有时会光顾洛杉矶的夜总会，并客串鼓手替人打鼓，但 Feynman 教授本人告诉我事实并非如此。他的另一项绝活则是开保险箱。

cues.en: One legend says that he once opened a lock safe in a secret establishment, removed the secret document, and left a note saying, guess who? I could tell you about the time that he learned Spanish before he went to give a series of lectures in Brazil, but I won't. This gives you enough background, I think, so let me say that I'm delighted to welcome
cues.zh: 有个传说说，他曾在一家秘密机构里打开一个保险箱，取走秘密文件，还留了张纸条写着：猜猜是谁？我也可以讲讲他在去巴西做系列讲座之前学会西班牙语的事，但我不讲了。我想这些背景已经足够了，所以让我说，我很高兴欢迎

cues.en: Professor Feynman back to Cornell. His general topic is the nature of physical law, and his topic for tonight is the law of gravitation, an example of physical law. Professor Feynman. It's odd, but in the infrequent occasions when I've been called upon in a formal place to play the bongo drums, the introducer never seems to find it necessary to mention that I also do theoretical physics. I believe that's probably a...
cues.zh: Feynman教授回到Cornell。他的总主题是物理定律的本质，今晚的主题是引力定律——物理定律的一个例子。Feynman教授。说来也怪，在我偶尔被请到正式场合演奏邦戈鼓时，介绍人似乎从不觉得有必要提到我也做理论物理。我想这大概是……

cues.en: that we respect the arts more than the sciences. The artists of the Renaissance said that man's main concern should be for man, and yet there are some other things of interest in the world. Even the artists appreciate sunsets and the ocean waves and the march of the stars across the heavens, and there is some reason then to talk of other things sometimes. As we look into these things,
cues.zh: 也就是说，我们尊重艺术甚于科学。文艺复兴时期的艺术家说，人主要关心的应该是人，但世界上还有一些其他有趣的东西。就连艺术家也欣赏日落、海浪和群星划过天空的运行，所以有时也有理由谈谈别的东西。当我们观察这些东西时，

cues.en: We get an aesthetic pleasure from them directly on observation. But there's also a rhythm and a pattern between the phenomena of nature, which isn't apparent to the eye, but only to the eye of analysis. And it's these rhythms and patterns which we call physical laws. What I want to talk about in a series of lectures is the general characteristics of these physical laws. That's even another level, if you will, of higher generality over the laws themselves.
cues.zh: 我们直接观察它们时，会得到一种审美愉悦。但自然现象之间还有一种节奏和模式，它不是肉眼能看见的，只有分析之眼才能看见。而我们把这些节奏和模式称为物理定律。我在系列讲座中想谈的，是这些物理定律的一般特征。可以说，这甚至是另一个层次，比定律本身具有更高的普遍性。

cues.en: really why I'm talking about is nature as seen as a result of detailed analysis, but only the most overall general qualities of nature is what I mainly wish to speak about. Now such a topic has a tendency to become too philosophical because it becomes so general that a person talks in such generalities that everybody can understand him and it's considered to be some deep philosophy. However, I would like to be rather more special and
cues.zh: 我真正要谈的，是经过细致分析后所看到的自然，但我主要想讲的只是自然最总体、最一般的性质。现在，这样的主题容易变得过于哲学化，因为它太一般了，一个人讲得如此泛泛，人人都能听懂，就被认为是某种深奥哲学。不过，我更想更具体一些，并且

cues.en: I would like to be understood in an honest way rather than in a vague way to some extent. And so if you don't mind, I'm going to try to give, instead of only the generalities, in this first lecture an example of physical law so that you have at least one example of the things about which I am speaking generally. In this way, I can use this example again and again to give an instance to make a reality out of something which will otherwise be too abstract.
cues.zh: 我希望在某种程度上，人们能诚实地理解我，而不是模糊地理解我。所以，如果你不介意，在这第一讲里，我不只讲一般性，而要试着给出一个物理定律的例子，这样你至少有一个例子，能说明我一般性谈论的那些东西。这样一来，我就能反复使用这个例子，给出具体实例，让本来会过于抽象的东西变得真实。

cues.en: Now, I've chosen for my special example of physical law to tell you about the theory of gravitation or the phenomena of gravity. Why I chose gravity, I don't know. Whatever I chose, you would ask the same question. Actually, it was one of the first great laws to be discovered and that has an interesting history. You might say yes, but then it's all had. I would like to hear something about science, more modern science. More recent, perhaps, but not more modern.
cues.zh: 现在，我选了一个物理定律的典型例子，来给大家讲讲引力理论或重力现象。至于为什么选引力，我也说不上来。反正不管我选什么，你们都会问同样的问题。事实上，它是人类最早发现的伟大定律之一，其背后有着一段非常有趣的历史。你可能会说：好吧，但这都是老黄历了，我想听点科学，更现代的科学。或许是年代更新一些，但绝称不上更现代。

cues.en: Modern science is exactly in the same tradition as the discoveries of the law of gravitation. It is only more recent discoveries that we would be talking about. And so I have no, I do not feel at all bad about telling you of the law of gravitation because I am in describing its history and the methods, the character of its discovery and its quality, talking about modern science, completely modern. This law has been called the greatest generalization achieved by the human mind.
cues.zh: 现代科学与引力定律的发现，完全是一脉相承的。如果我们聊别的，充其量也就是发现的时间更近一些而已。所以，跟大家讲万有引力定律，我一点也不觉得过时，因为在描述它的历史、研究方法、发现过程的特质及其内涵时，我谈论的正是现代科学，彻彻底底的现代科学。这个定律曾被誉为人类思维所达到的最伟大的概括。

cues.en: And you can get already by introduction, I'm more interested, not so much in the human mind, as in the marble of nature who can obey such an elegant and simple law as this law of gravitation. So our main concentration will not be on how clever we are to have found it all out, but on how clever she is to pay attention to it. Now, what is this law of gravitation that we're going to talk about? The law is that
cues.zh: 从开场白中你们就能看出来，相比于人类的心智，我更着迷于大自然的鬼斧神工——她竟然能遵循如此优雅而简朴的引力定律。因此，我们关注的重点不会放在人类有多聪明才发现了它，而是大自然有多奇妙，竟然能严丝合缝地遵循它。那么，我们今天要讲的这个引力定律到底是什么呢？这个定律的内容是：

cues.en: Two bodies, or bodies exert a force upon each other, which is inversely as the square of the distance between them, and varies directly as the product of their masses. And mathematically, we can write that great law down in the formula, some kind of a constant times the product of the two masses divided by the square of the distance. Now if I add the remark that a body reacts to a force by accelerating, or by changing its velocity every second,
cues.zh: 两个物体之间会相互施加引力，该力与它们之间距离的平方成反比，并与它们质量的乘积成正比。在数学上，我们可以把这个伟大的定律写成一个公式：某个常数乘以两个物体质量的乘积，再除以距离的平方。如果我再加上一条：物体在受到外力时会产生加速度，也就是每秒改变其速度，

cues.en: to an extent inversely as its mass. It reacts, changes velocity more if the mass is lower and so on, inversely as the mass. Then I have said everything about the law of gravitation that needs to be said. Everything else is a consequence, a mathematical consequence of those two things that I said. That's a remarkable enough phenomenon in itself that the next lecture will consider this in more detail.
cues.zh: 其改变的程度与物体的质量成反比。也就是说，质量越小，速度改变得越剧烈，反之亦然，与质量成反比。那么关于引力定律，该讲的我就全都讲完了。剩下的所有现象，都不过是我刚才说的这两点的数学推论而已。这本身就是一个极其非凡的现象，下一讲我们还会对此进行更详细的讨论。

cues.en: Now, I know you're not all here. I know some of you are, but you're not all mathematicians. And so you cannot all immediately see all of the consequences of these two remarks. And so what I would like to do in this lecture is to briefly tell you the story of the discovery, tell you what some of the consequences are, what the effect of this discovery had on the history of science, what kinds of mysteries such a law entails, something about the refinements made by Einstein, and possibly the relation to other laws of physics.
cues.zh: 我知道台下的各位——我知道你们有些人是，但并非所有人都是数学家。所以你们不可能立刻看出这两点所推导出的所有结论。因此，在今天的演讲中，我希望能简要地给大家讲讲这个发现的故事，聊聊它的一些推论，这项发现对科学史产生了怎样的影响，这样的定律背后蕴含着怎样的奥秘，Einstein 对它做出了哪些修正，以及它与其他物理定律之间可能存在的联系。

cues.en: The history of the thing, as briefly as this, that the ancients first observed the way the planets seemed to move about in the sky, and concluded that they all went around, along with the Earth, went around the sun. This discovery was later made independently by Copernicus, if they had forgotten, people had forgotten that it had already been made. Now the next thing, question that came up to study was exactly how do they go around the sun? That is,
cues.zh: 这件事的历史，简短说就是这样：古人首先观察到行星似乎在天空中移动的方式，并得出结论：它们和地球一样，全都绕着太阳转。这个发现后来被 Copernicus 独立做出——如果古人忘了，人们已经忘了这个发现早已做出。接下来出现要研究的问题是：它们究竟如何绕太阳转？也就是，

cues.en: exactly what kind of motion. Do they go with the Sun at the center of a circle or do they go in some other kind of a curve? How fast do they move and so on? And this discovery took a longer to make. The times after Copernicus were times in which there were great debates about whether the planets in fact went around the Sun along with the Earth or whether the Earth was at the center of the universe and so on, and there were considerable arguments about this.
cues.zh: 究竟是什么样的运动。它们是太阳在圆心作圆周运动，还是沿某种其他曲线运动？它们运动多快等等？这个发现花了更长时间才做出。Copernicus 之后的时代，人们对行星是否真的和地球一起绕太阳转，还是地球位于宇宙中心等等，有过激烈争论，围绕这个问题有相当多的争论。

cues.en: When a man named Tycho Bray got an idea, a way of answering the question, he thought that it might perhaps be a good idea to look very, very carefully and to record where the planets actually appear in the sky, and then the alternative theories might be distinguished from one another. This is the key of modern science and is the beginning of the true understanding of nature, this idea.
cues.zh: 一个叫 Tycho Bray 的人想到一个主意，一种回答这个问题的方法：他认为，也许一个好办法是极其仔细地观察，并记录行星在天空中实际出现的位置，然后不同的理论也许就能彼此区分。这就是现代科学的关键，也是真正理解自然的开端，就是这个想法：

cues.en: that to look at the thing, to record the details, and to hope that in the information thus obtained may lie a clue to one or another of a possible theoretical interpretation. So Tycho, who was a rich man and owned, I believe, an island near Copenhagen, outfitted his island with great brass circles and special observing positions, situations, chairs that you could look through little holes, and recorded night after night
cues.zh: 要观察事物、记录细节，并希望由此获得的信息中，可能藏着指向某种可能理论解释的线索。于是 Tycho，他很有钱，我相信他在哥本哈根附近拥有一座岛，他在岛上装备了大型黄铜圆环、特殊的观测位置、可以透过小孔观察的椅子，一夜又一夜地记录

cues.en: the position of the planets. It's only through such hard work that we can find out anything. When all these data were collected, they came into the hands of Kepler, who then tried to analyze what kinds of motions the planets made around the Sun. And he did this by a method of trial and error. At one stage he thought he had it. He figured out that they went around the Sun in circles with the Sun off-center.
cues.zh: 行星的位置。只有通过这样艰苦的工作，我们才能发现任何东西。当所有这些数据收集起来后，交到了 Kepler 手中，他随后试图分析行星绕太阳做的是什么样的运动。他通过试错法来做。有一个阶段他以为搞定了。他推算出它们以太阳偏离圆心的圆周绕太阳转。

cues.en: And notice that one planet, I think it was Mars, but I don't know, was eight minutes of arc off. And he decided this was too big for Tycho Bray to have made an error and that this was not the right answer. So because of the precision of experiments, he was able to proceed and find that to go on to another trial and found, in fact, ultimately this. Three things. First, that the planets went in ellipses around the sun with the sun at a focus. In ellipses, a curve, you had
cues.zh: 注意有一颗行星，我想是火星，但我不确定，差了八弧分。他判定这个误差太大，不可能是 Tycho Bray 犯的错，所以这不是正确答案。因此，由于实验的精确性，他能够继续，进行另一次尝试，并最终发现实际上是这样。三点。第一，行星沿椭圆绕太阳转，太阳位于一个焦点上。椭圆，这种曲线，你——

cues.en: All artists know about because it's a foreshortened circle, when children know about because somebody told them that if you take a string and tie it to two tacks and put a pencil in there, it'll make an ellipse. These two tacks are the foci, and if the sun is here, the shape of the orbit of a planet around the sun is one of these curves. The next question is, in going around the ellipse, how does it go? Does it go faster when it's near the sun, slower when it's further from the sun, and so on?
cues.zh: 所有艺术家都知道它，因为它是透视缩短的圆；孩子们也知道，因为有人告诉过他们，拿一根绳子系在两个图钉上，把铅笔放进去，就会画出一个椭圆。这两个图钉就是焦点；如果太阳在这里，那么行星绕太阳的轨道形状就是这些曲线之一。下一个问题是：沿椭圆绕行时，它怎么走？靠近太阳时更快，离太阳更远时更慢，等等吗？

cues.en: We take away the other focus, we have the Sun then and the planet going around, and Kepler found the answer to this too. He found this, that if you put the position of the planet down at two times separated by some definite time, let's say three weeks, and then at another place in the orbit, put the positions of the planets again separated by three weeks, and draw lines from the Sun to the planet, technically called radius vectors.
cues.zh: 我们拿掉另一个焦点，就只剩下太阳和绕着它转的行星，而开普勒也解开了这个谜题。他发现，如果你记下相隔特定时间（比如三周）的两个行星位置，然后在轨道的另一处，同样记下相隔三周的行星位置，并从太阳向行星画线——术语叫径矢。

cues.en: Anyway, lines from the sun to the planet. Then the area that's enclosed in the orbit of the planet and the two lines that are separated by the planet's position three weeks apart is the same no matter what part of the orbit the thing is on. So that it has to go faster when it's closer in order to get the same area as it goes slower when it's further away and in this precise manner. Some several years later he found the third rule
cues.zh: 不管怎么说，就是从太阳连到行星的线。那么，由行星轨道和相隔三周的这两条线所围成的面积，无论它处于轨道的哪一段都是相同的。因此，它在离太阳更近时必须运行得更快，才能扫过与离得较远、走得较慢时相同的面积，并且遵循这种精确的方式。几年后，他又发现了第三条定律。

cues.en: And that had not to do with the exactly motion of a single planet around the Sun, but related the various planets to each other. And it said that the times that took the planet to go all the way around was related to the size of the orbit, and that the times went as the square root of the cube of the size of the orbit, and for the size of the orbit is the diameter all the way across the biggest distance on the ellipse.
cues.zh: 这条定律与单个行星绕太阳运行的精确运动无关，而是将不同行星彼此联系了起来。它指出，行星公转一周所需的时间与轨道大小相关，而且公转时间与轨道大小的三次方根成正比——这里的轨道大小是指椭圆上最长跨度的直径。

cues.en: He has these three laws which are summarized by saying it's an ellipse, and that equal areas are swept in equal times, and that the time to go around varies as a three-half power of the size, the square root of the cube of the size, so it's three laws of Kepler, which is a very complete description of the motion of the planets around the Sun. The next question was, what makes them go around? Well, how can we understand this in more detail?
cues.zh: 他总结出了这三条定律：轨道是椭圆；相等时间内扫过相等的面积；公转时间与轨道大小的二分之三次方（即大小的三次方根）成正比。这就是开普勒三定律，它非常完整地描述了行星绕太阳的运动。接下来的问题是：是什么驱使它们运转的？我们又该如何更深入地理解这一点？

cues.en: Or is there anything else to say? In the meantime, Galileo was investigating the laws of motion. Incidentally, at the time of Kepler, the problem of what drove the planets around the Sun was answered by some people by saying that there were angels behind here beating their wings and pushing the planet around orbit. As we'll see, that that answer is not very far from the truth. The only difference is that the angels sit in a different direction and
cues.zh: 或者还有什么要补充的吗？与此同时，Galileo 正在研究运动定律。顺便提一句，在开普勒那个时代，对于什么驱使行星绕太阳运转的问题，有些人的回答是：有天使在行星身后扇动翅膀，推着它沿轨道前行。正如我们即将看到的，这个答案其实离真相并不太远。唯一的区别在于，天使所处的位置方向不同，以及

cues.en: where wings go to. But the point that the angels sit in a different direction is the one that I must now come to. Galileo, in studying the laws of motion and doing a number of experiments of seeing how balls rolled down inclined planes and pendulous swung and so on, discovered a idealization, a great principle called the principle of inertia, which is this.
cues.zh: 翅膀朝向何处。但关键在于天使处于不同的方向，这也是我现在必须讲到的。Galileo 在研究运动定律的过程中，做了大量实验，观察小球如何沿斜面滚下、钟摆如何摆动等等，由此发现了一种理想化模型，一个被称为惯性定律的伟大原理，它是这样的。

cues.en: that if a thing has nothing acting on it, if an object has nothing acting on it and is going along at a certain velocity in a straight line, it will go at the same velocity at exactly the same straight line forever. Unbelievable though that may sound to anybody who has tried to make a ball roll forever, the idealization is correct and that if there were no influences acting such as the friction on the floor and so on, the thing would go at a uniform speed forever. The next point was made by Newton.
cues.zh: 如果一个物体不受任何作用，如果它以一定速度沿直线运动，它就会永远以同样的速度沿同一条直线运动。对任何试过让球一直滚下去的人来说，这听起来也许难以置信，但这种理想化是正确的：如果没有摩擦力之类的影响，物体就会永远匀速运动。下一点由牛顿提出。

cues.en: who discussed the next question, which is, when it doesn't go in a straight line, then what? And they answered this way, that a force is needed to change the velocity in any manner. First, for instance, if you're pushing it in a direction that it moves, it will speed up. If you find that it changes direction, then the force must have been sideways. And that the force can be measured by the product of two effects. First, how much does the velocity change?
cues.zh: 他讨论了下个问题：当它不走直线时，那会怎样？他们的回答是：要以任何方式改变速度，都需要力。首先，比如你沿它运动的方向推它，它就会加速。如果你发现它改变了方向，那力一定是侧向的。力可以通过两种效应的乘积来量度。第一，速度改变了多少？

cues.en: small interval of time. How fast is the velocity changing? How much is it accelerating in this direction, or how much is the velocity changing when it changes direction? That's called the acceleration. And when that's multiplied by a coefficient called the mass of an object, or it's inertia coefficient, then that together is a force. One can measure the, for instance, if one has a stone on the end of a string and swings it in the circle over his head, then one can measure, everyone finds one has to pull. The reason is that the speed of this
cues.zh: 在一小段时间内。速度变化得多快？它在这个方向上加速多少，或者当它改变方向时速度变化多少？这叫作加速度。当它乘以一个叫物体质量的系数，或者叫惯性系数，那么合起来就是力。可以测量——例如，如果一个人把石头系在绳子一端，在头顶上转圈，那么可以测量，每个人都会发现自己得拉绳子。原因是，这个物体的速度

cues.en: The velocity, the speed is not changing as it goes around the circle, but it's changing its direction, so there must be perpetually an infalling force. And this is proportional to the mass, so that if we were to take two different objects, first swing one, and then swing another one at the same speed around the head and measure the force in the second one, that second one, the new force is bigger than the other force in the proportion that the masses are different. This is a way of measuring the masses. By how much, how hard it is
cues.zh: 速度、速率在绕圈时并没有改变，但方向在改变，所以必定始终有一个向内的力。这个力与质量成正比，因此如果我们拿两个不同的物体，先转一个，再以同样速度在头顶转另一个，并测量第二个物体上的力，那么第二个的新力会更大，其比例与质量差异相同。这就是测量质量的一种方法。通过需要多大、多难

cues.en: to change the speed. Now, then Newton saw, I from this, that for instance, to take a simple example, if a planet is going in a circle around the sun, no force is needed to make it go sideways tangentially. If there were no force at all on it, it would have just keep coasting this way. But actually, the planet doesn't keep coasting this way, but finds itself later, not out here, where it would go if there were no force at all.
cues.zh: 才能改变速度。然后牛顿从中看出，举例来说，举个简单的例子，如果一颗行星绕太阳做圆周运动，不需要力让它沿切线方向侧向运动。如果它完全不受力，它就会一直这样滑行。但实际上，行星并不会一直这样滑行，而是后来发现自己不在外面这里——如果完全不受力它本会去的地方。

cues.en: but further down toward the sun. In other words, its velocity, its motion has been deflected toward the sun. So what the angels have to do is to beat their wings in toward the sun all the time. That the motion to keep it going in a straight line has no known reason. The reason why things coast forever has never been found out. The law of inertia is no known origin. So the angels
cues.zh: 而是更靠近太阳下方。换句话说，它的速度、它的运动被偏向了太阳。所以天使要做的，就是一直朝太阳方向扇动翅膀。让物体保持直线运动，并没有已知的原因。物体为什么永远滑行，从未被查明。惯性定律没有已知起源。所以天使

cues.en: don't exist, but the continuation of the motion does. But in order to obtain the falling operation, we do need a force. So it became apparent that the origin of that the force was toward the sun. As a matter of fact, Newton was able to demonstrate that the statement that equal areas are swept in equal times was a direct consequence of the simple idea that all of the changes in velocity are directed exactly to the sun, even in the elliptical case.
cues.zh: 并不存在，但运动的延续确实存在。不过为了得到下落运动，我们确实需要力。于是很明显，这个力的来源指向太阳。事实上，牛顿能够证明，“相等时间扫过相等面积”这一说法，直接源于一个简单观念：所有速度变化都恰好指向太阳，即使在椭圆情形下也是如此。

cues.en: and maybe I'll have time next time to show you how that works in detail. So from this law, he would confirm the idea that the force is toward the Sun. And from knowing how the periods of the different planets vary with the distance away from the Sun, it's possible to determine how that force must weaken at different distances, and he was able to determine that the force must vary inversely as the square of the distance. Now so far he hasn't said anything, yes, because he only said two things which
cues.zh: 也许下次我会有时间向大家详细展示它的运作原理。从这一定律出发，他证实了引力是指向太阳的这一观点。而且通过了解不同行星的公转周期如何随与太阳的距离而变化，就能够确定这种力在不同距离下必然是如何减弱的，于是他推导出力必定与距离的平方成反比。不过到目前为止，他其实还没提出什么全新的见解，对吧，因为他说的不过是

cues.en: Kepler said, in a different language, one is exactly equivalent to the statement that the force is toward the sun, and the other is exactly equivalent to the statement that the law is inversely as the square of the distance. But people had seen in telescopes the Jupiter's satellites going around Jupiter, and it looked like a little solar system. So the satellites were attracted to Jupiter, and the moon is attracted to the Earth, and this goes around the Earth, is attracted the same way. So it looks like everything's attracted to everything else. And so the next statement was to generalize this and to say that every object attracts every other object.
cues.zh: 开普勒用另一种语言表达过的两件事：一件完全等同于“力指向太阳”的说法，另一件完全等同于“引力大小与距离平方成反比”的定律。但当时人们已经通过望远镜观察到了木星的卫星绕着木星转，看起来就像个微型太阳系。也就是说卫星被木星吸引，月球被地球吸引并绕着地球转，受力方式也是一样的。看来任何物体都会吸引其他所有物体。于是接下来的结论就是将其推广，认为每一个物体都会吸引其他任何物体。

cues.en: If so, the Earth must be pulling on the Moon just as the Sun pulls on the planet. But it's known that the Earth pulls on things because you're all sitting tightly in your seats in spite of your desires to float out of the hall at this time. The pull for objects on the Earth was well known in the phenomenon of gravitation. And it was Newton's idea then that maybe the gravitation which held the Moon in the orbit also applied was the same gravitation that pulled the objects toward the Earth.
cues.zh: 如果是这样，地球对月球的引力必然就像太阳对行星的引力一样。但地球会吸引物体是众所周知的，因为尽管大家此刻可能想飘出大厅，但都还好好地坐在椅子上。地球对物体的引力就是广为人知的重力现象。当时牛顿的想法是，让月球保持在轨道上的引力，也许跟把物体拉向地面的引力其实是同一种力。

cues.en: Now it is easy to figure out how far the moon falls in one second. Because if it went in a straight line, you know the size of the orbit, you know it takes a month to go around. And if you figure out how far it goes in one second, you can figure out how far the circle of the moon's orbit has fallen below the straight line that it would have been in if it didn't go the way it does go. And this distance is one-twentieth of an inch. Now the moon is sixty
cues.zh: 现在要算出月球在一秒内“下落”了多少距离其实很容易。因为如果它沿直线飞行，我们知道轨道的尺寸，也知道它绕一圈需要一个月。只要算出一秒钟它前进了多远，就能算出月球轨道的圆弧比它不拐弯时原本所在的直线下降了多少。这个距离是二十分之一英寸。而月球距离地心的距离是我们的

cues.en: Times as far away from the Earth's center than we are. We're 4,000 miles away from the center and the moon is 240,000 miles away from the center. So if the law of inverse square is right, an object at the Earth's surface should fall in one second by on 20th of an inch times 3600 being the square of 60 because the force has been weakened by 60 times 60 for the inverse square law in getting out there to the moon.
cues.zh: 六十倍。我们距离地心有 4000 英里，而月球距离地心有 240,000 英里。因此如果平方反比定律是正确的，地表上的物体在一秒内的下落距离应该是二十分之一英寸乘以 3600（即 60 的平方），因为根据平方反比定律，远在月球处的引力已经被削弱了 60 乘以 60 倍。

cues.en: And if you multiply a 20th of an inch by 3600, you get about 16 feet. And low, it is known already, from Galileo's measurements, that things fell in one second on the Earth's surface by 16 feet. So this meant, you see, that he was on the right track. There was no going back now. Because a new fact that was completely independent previously, which is the period of the moon's orbit and its distance from the Earth, was connected to another fact, which is how long it takes something to fall in one second.
cues.zh: 如果把 1/20 英寸乘以 3600，就得到大约 16 英尺。瞧，从伽利略的测量中已经知道，地球表面的物体一秒下落 16 英尺。所以你看，这意味着他走对了路。现在已经无法回头了。因为此前完全独立的一个新事实——月球轨道的周期以及月球到地球的距离——被联系到了另一个事实上：物体下落一秒需要多长时间。

cues.en: But this was a dramatic test that everything's all right. Further, he had a lot of other predictions. He was able to calculate what the shape of the orbit should be if the law were the inverse square and found, indeed, that it was an ellipse. So he got three for two, as it were. In addition, a number of new phenomena had obvious explanations. One was the tides. The tides were due to the pull of the moon on the Earth. This had sometimes been thought of before.
cues.zh: 但这是一次戏剧性的检验，证明一切都没问题。此外，他还有很多其他预言。他能算出如果定律是平方反比，轨道应该是什么形状，并且发现它确实是椭圆。所以可以说，他一下子得到三样收获。另外，许多新现象都有了显然的解释。其中之一是潮汐。潮汐是由月球对地球的引力造成的。这一点以前有时也有人想到过。

cues.en: with the difficulty that if it's the pull of the moon on the Earth, the Earth being here, the water's being pulled up to the moon, then there would only be one tide a day where that bump of water is under the moon. But actually, you know, there are tides every 12 hours, roughly, and that's two tides a day, but there was also another school of thought that had a different conclusion. Their theory was that it was the Earth that was pulled by the moon away from the water.
cues.zh: 但有个困难：如果是月球把地球往自己这边拉，地球在这里，水被拉向月球，那么一天只会有一个潮汐，也就是水隆起处在月球下方的时候。但实际你知道，大约每 12 小时就有一次潮汐，也就是一天两次潮汐。不过还有另一派想法得出了不同结论。他们的理论是：是月球把地球拉离了水。

cues.en: So actually, Newton was the first one to realize what actually was going on. That the force of the moon on the Earth and on the water is the same at the same distance, and that the water here is closer to the moon, and the water here is further from the moon than the Earth, than the rigid Earth, so that the water is pulled more toward the moon here, and here is less toward the moon than the Earth, so there's a combination of those two pictures that makes it double tight. Actually, the Earth
cues.zh: 所以实际上，牛顿是第一个意识到真正发生了什么的人。月球对地球和对水的力在相同距离下是一样的；这里的水比地球、比刚性的地球更靠近月球，而这里的水比地球更远离月球。所以这里的水被更多地拉向月球，那里的水则比地球更少地被拉向月球。于是这两幅图景结合起来，就形成了双重潮汐。实际上，地球

cues.en: does the same trick as the moon. It goes around a circle, really. I mean, the force of the moon on the Earth is balanced, but by what? By the fact that just like the moon goes in a circle to balance the Earth's force, the Earth is also going in a circle. Actually, the center of the circle is somewhere inside the Earth. It's also going in a circle to balance the moon. So the two of them go around a common center here. And if you wish, this water is thrown off by centrifugal force more than the Earth is, and this water is attracted.
cues.zh: 也像月球一样玩同样的把戏。它其实在绕圈。我是说，月球对地球的力被平衡了，但被什么平衡？靠的是：就像月球绕圈以平衡地球的力，地球也在绕圈。实际上，这个圆的中心在地球内部某处。它也在绕圈以平衡月球。所以两者绕着一个共同中心运动。你也可以这么理解：这里的水比地球更被离心力甩出去，而这里的水受到吸引。

cues.en: more than the average of the Earth. At any rate, the tides were then explained, and the fact that there were two a day. A lot of other things became quite clear why the Earth is round, because everything gets pulled in, and why it isn't round, because it's spinning so that the outside gets thrown out a little bit and it balances, and why the sun and moon are round, and so on. Now, as the science developed,
cues.zh: 比地球的平均值更多。不管怎样，潮汐以及一天两次潮汐这一事实，随后都得到了解释。许多其他事情也变得相当清楚：地球为什么是圆的，因为一切都被向内拉；又为什么不是完美的球形，因为它在自转，外侧被稍微甩出去并达到平衡；以及太阳和月亮为什么是圆的，等等。后来，随着科学的发展，

cues.en: And measurements were made ever more accurately. The tests of Newton's law became much more stringent. And the first careful tests involved the moons of Jupiter. By careful observations of the way they went around over a long period of time, one could be very careful to check that everything was according to Newton. It turned out not to be the case. The moons of Jupiter appeared to be first to get sometimes to eight minutes ahead of time and sometimes eight minutes behind our schedule, where schedule is the calculated values.
cues.zh: 测量也变得越来越精确。对牛顿定律的检验变得严格得多。最早的一批仔细检验涉及木星的卫星。通过长期仔细观测它们绕行方式，人们可以非常仔细地检查一切都符合牛顿定律。结果却并非如此。木星的卫星似乎偏快，有时比预定时间早八分钟，有时又比我们的时间表晚八分钟，而时间表就是计算值。

cues.en: according to Newton's laws. It was noticed that they were ahead of schedule when they were close, when Jupiter was close to the Earth and behind schedule when it was far away, rather hard circumstance. And Mr. Rumer, having confidence in the law of gravitation, came to an interesting conclusion, that it takes light some time to travel from the moons to the Earth, and that what we're looking at when we see the moons are not how they are now, but how they were the time ago that it took the light to get here now when Jupiter's near us,
cues.zh: 根据牛顿定律，人们注意到，当它们靠近时——即木星靠近地球时——它们比预期提前了，而当它远离时则滞后了，这是相当棘手的情况。而对引力定律深信不疑的 Romer 先生得出了一个有趣的结论：光从这些卫星传到地球是需要时间的，我们看到卫星时的样子，并非它们此刻的模样，而是光传到这里所需时间之前的样子；现在当木星离我们较近时，

cues.en: it takes less time for the light to come, and when Jupiter's further, it takes longer time, so he had to correct the observations for the differences in time, and by the fact that they were this much too early, or that much too late, was able to determine the velocity of light. This was the first demonstration that light was not an instantaneously propagating material. I bring this particular matter to your attention because it illustrates something. That when a law is right, it can be used to find another one.
cues.zh: 光传过来耗时较短，而当木星更远时耗时更长，因此他必须根据时间差异对观测结果进行修正，并且通过它们提前或滞后了多少这一事实，成功测定了光速。这是首次证明光并非瞬时传播的物质。我之所以特意提这件事，是因为它说明了一个道理：当一条定律是正确的时候，它可以用来发现另一条定律。

cues.en: By having confidence in this law, if something is the matter, it suggests perhaps some other phenomenon. And if we had not known the law of gravitation, we would have taken much longer to find the speed of light, because we would not have known what to expect of Jupiter's satellites. This process has developed into an avalanche of discoveries. Each new discovery permits the tools for much more discovery, and this is the beginning of that avalanche, which has gone on now for 400 years in a continuous process.
cues.zh: 正是因为对这条定律有信心，如果出现了反常，就暗示着或许存在其他现象。如果我们当时不知道万有引力定律，发现光速就会花上长得多的时间，因为我们根本不知道木星的卫星该呈现出什么规律。这一过程演变成了发现的雪崩效应。每一个新发现都为更多的发现提供了工具，而这正是那场雪崩的开端，如今它已持续了400年，从未间断。

cues.en: and we're still avalanching along at high speed at this time. Another problem came up. The planets shouldn't really go in ellipses, because according to Newton's laws, they're not attracted only by the Sun, but also they pull on each other a little bit. Only a little bit, but a little bit is something, and we'll alter the motion a little bit. So Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus were big planets that were known, and the calculations were made as to how slightly different than the perfect ellipses of Kepler the planets ought to be going. Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus.
cues.zh: 而且此刻我们仍在这场雪崩中高速前行。接着又出现了一个新问题：行星其实不应该严格按椭圆轨道运行，因为根据牛顿定律，它们不仅受到太阳的引力，彼此之间也会有一点点相互拉扯。虽然只有一点点，但这微小的影响也是存在的，会让运动发生轻微改变。当时已知的几颗大行星有木星、土星和天王星，科学家们便计算了行星轨道与 Kepler 完美椭圆轨道之间的微小偏差，也就是木星、土星和天王星

cues.en: by the pull of one on each other. And when they were finished, the calculations I mean, and the observations, it was noticed that Jupiter and Saturn went according to the calculations, but that Uranus was doing something funny. Another opportunity for Newton's laws to be found wanting, but courage. Two men, both who made these calculations, Adams and Laverrier, independently and at almost exactly the same time, proposed that the motions of Uranus were due to an unseen as yet new planet.
cues.zh: 因彼此相互牵引而产生的偏差。当一切搞定后——我是指计算和观测——人们发现木星和土星的运行完全符合计算，但天王星却有些不对劲。这本是证明牛顿定律存在缺陷的又一次机会，但有人展现了勇气。两位进行这些计算的人，Adams 和 Leverrier，各自独立且几乎在同一时间提出，天王星的异常运动源于一颗尚未被发现的新行星。

cues.en: And they wrote letters to their respective observatories telling them to look. Turn your telescope and look there and you'll find a planet. How absurd, said one of the observatories that some guy sitting with pieces of paper and pencils can tell us where we'd look to find something new planet. And the other observatory was more, well less, well, the administration was different. And they found the Neptune.
cues.zh: 他们写信给各自的天文台，让他们去看。“把望远镜转过去，看那里，你就会发现一颗行星。”其中一家天文台说，一个拿着纸笔坐着的家伙，居然能告诉我们该往哪儿找新行星，太荒唐了。另一家天文台则更……嗯，没那么……反正管理方式不一样。结果他们发现了海王星。

cues.en: More recently, in the beginning of the 20th century, it became apparent that the motion of the planet Mercury was not exactly right. So the force of attraction on an object is exactly proportional to its coefficient of inertia. In other words, it's mass. I should say something about the relation of gravitation to other forces, to other parts of nature, other phenomena in nature. And I'll have more to say of a general quality later. But there is one
cues.zh: 在这样的精度下没有偏转。所以我们知道，太阳对这两个物体的引力正好与它们的离心效应成正比，也就是与惯性成正比。因此，物体所受的引力正好与它的惯性系数成正比，换句话说，就是与其质量成正比。我应该谈谈引力与其他力、自然界其他部分以及其他自然现象之间的关系。稍后我还会就其普遍性质多讲一些。但有一点

cues.en: thing that's particularly interesting, and that is that the inverse square law appears again. It appears in the electrical laws, for instance, that electricity also exerts forces inversely as the square of the distance, this time between charges. And one thinks perhaps inverse square of the distance has some deep significance. Maybe gravity and electricity are different aspects of the same thing. No one has ever succeeded in making gravity and electricity different aspects of the same thing. Today, our theories of physics, the laws of physics,
cues.zh: 特别有趣，那就是平方反比定律再次出现了。比如在电学定律中就出现了，电荷之间施加的作用力同样与距离的平方成反比。人们可能会想，与距离平方成反比或许有某种深刻的意义，也许引力和电是同一事物的不同表象。但从来没有人成功证明引力和电是同一事物的不同方面。今天，我们的物理理论、物理定律，

cues.en: are a multitude of different parts and pieces that don't fit together very well. We don't understand the one exactly in terms of the other. We don't have one structure from which all is deduced. We have several pieces that don't quite fit exactly yet. And that's the reason why in these lectures, instead of having the ability to tell you what the law of physics is, I asked to talk about the things that are common to the various laws, because we don't know, we don't understand the connection between them. But what's very strange is that there are certain things that are the same in both.
cues.zh: 是由许多拼凑得不太好的零碎部分组成的。我们无法完全用一种理论去解释另一种理论，我们没有一个可以推导一切的统构体系，而是只有几块目前还没完全拼合的碎片。这就是为什么在这些讲座中，我无法直接告诉你那条唯一的物理定律是什么，而是不得不探讨各类定律之间的共通之处，因为我们不知道、也不理解它们之间的联系。但非常奇妙的是，它们之间确实存在某些共通的特质。

cues.en: But now let's look again at the law of electricity. The law goes inversely as the square of the distance. But the thing that is remarkable is the tremendous difference in the strength of the electrical and gravitational laws. People who want to make electricity and gravitation out of the same thing will find that electricity is so much more powerful than gravity that it's hard to believe they could both have the same origin. Now how can I say one thing is more powerful than another? It depends upon how much charge you have and how much mass you have. I'm certainly
cues.zh: 现在让我们再来看看电学定律。这条定律也是与距离的平方成反比。但引人注目的是，电学定律和引力定律的强度存在着巨大的悬殊。那些想把电和引力归为同一种事物的人会发现，电比引力强大得多，很难让人相信它们会源自同一个起点。那我凭什么说一种力比另一种力更强呢？这取决于你有多少电荷和多少质量。我当然……

If we try to get something that nature produces her own pure number that has nothing to do with inches or years or anything to do with our own dimensions, we can do it this way. If we take the fundamental particles such as an electron, any different ones will give different numbers, but to get an idea of the number, take electrons.
cues.zh: 你不能通过说“我取了这么大一块东西”来谈论引力有多强，因为这个尺寸是你选定的。如果我们想得到一个由大自然本身产生的纯数，与英寸、年或我们自身的任何尺度都无关，我们可以这样做：如果我们取基本粒子，比如电子——虽然不同的粒子会得出不同的数字，但为了了解这个量级，我们就以电子为例。

cues.en: Two electrons are fundamental particles. It's an object. It's not something I can't... I don't have to tell you what units I measure in. It's two particles that are fundamental particles. They repel each other inversely as a square of the distance due to electricity. And they attract each other inversely as a square of the distance due to gravitation. Question. What is the ratio of the gravitational force to the electrical force? And that is illustrated on the next slide. The ratio of the gravitational attraction to the electrical repulsion is given by a number with 42 digits.
cues.zh: 两个电子都是基本粒子。这是客观存在的物体。我不需要……我甚至不用说明测量单位。它们就是两个基本粒子。因为电荷，它们相互排斥，力与距离的平方成反比。而因为万有引力，它们相互吸引，力同样与距离的平方成反比。问题来了：引力与电力的比值是多少？下一张幻灯片展示了这个结果。引力吸引与电力排斥的比值，是一个长达42位的数字。

cues.en: and goes off here, it's all this is written very carefully out, so that's 42 digits. Now, therein lies a very deep mystery. Where could such a tremendous number come from? That means if you ever had a theory from which both of these things are to come, how could they come in such disproportion? From one equation has a solution which has, for one, two kinds of forces, an attraction and a repulsion with that fantastic ratio. People have looked for such a large ratio in other places.
cues.zh: 从这里一直延伸过去，全都写得清清楚楚，整整42位数。这里面隐藏着一个极深奥的谜团。这么庞大的一个数字到底从何而来？这意味着，如果将来有一种理论能同时推导这两种力，它们怎么会有如此悬殊的比例？同一个方程的解，怎么会同时导出两种力——一种吸引，一种排斥——且两者之间存在如此惊人的比例？人们曾在其他地方寻找过如此巨大的比值。

And if you want a large number, why not take the diameter of the universe to the diameter of a proton? Amazingly enough, it also is a number with 42 digits. And so an interesting proposal is made that this ratio is the same as the ratio of the size of the universe to the diameter of a proton. But the universe is expanding with time. And that would mean the gravitational constant is changing with time.
cues.zh: 大家都在寻找一个很大的数。比如，人们希望还能找到另一个大数。如果你想要个大数，何不拿宇宙的直径比上质子的直径呢？令人惊奇的是，它也是一个42位的数字。于是有人提出了一个有趣的假说：这个比值和宇宙尺寸与质子直径的比值是相等的。但宇宙是在随时间膨胀的。这岂不是意味着引力常数也会随着时间改变。

cues.en: And although that's a possibility, there's no evidence to indicate that it's in fact true, and there are several difficulties, I mean, partial indications that it doesn't, that the gravitational constant has not changed in that way. So this tremendous number remains a mystery. I must say to finish about the theory of gravitation two more things. One is that Einstein had to modify the laws of gravitation in accordance with his principles of relativity. The first was
cues.zh: 尽管存在这种可能，但目前没有任何证据表明它确实如此，而且还存在一些困难，我是说，部分迹象表明它并没有变，引力常数并未以那种方式改变。所以这个巨大的数字依然是个谜。关于引力理论，我还必须最后补充两点。第一点，爱因斯坦必须根据他的相对论原理来修正引力定律。首先是……

They have very small effects, these modifications. One of them is, all masses fall, light has energy, and energy is equivalent to mass, so light should fall, and it should mean that light going near the sun is deflected. It is. And also, the force of gravitation is slightly modified in his theory.
cues.zh: 原理之一是相互作用不能瞬时发生，而牛顿理论却认为引力是瞬时的。他不得不修正牛顿定律。这些修正带来的效应非常微弱。其中之一是：所有质量都会下落，光具有能量，而能量等价于质量，所以光也应该下落，这就意味着经过太阳附近的光线会发生偏折。事实确是如此。此外，在他的理论中，万有引力也发生了微小的修正。

cues.zh: 定律因此有了极其微小的改变，而这个改变量正好能够解释在水星运动中发现的微小偏差。最后，关于微观尺度上的物理定律，我们发现微观物质的行为遵循的规律，与宏观事物截然不同。那么问题来了：引力在微观尺度下又是什么样的？所谓的量子引力理论究竟是什么？目前还没有……

cues.zh: 然后决定按照那个规律来运动吗？”换句话说，虽然我给出了数学定律，却完全没有向你们揭示其中的机制。我将在下一讲探讨这方面的可能性，也就是数学与物理的关系。但在本讲的最后，我想强调一下引力与我们一路提到过的其他定律所具有的一些共同特征。

cues.en: The first is that it's mathematical in its expression. The others are that way too. We'll discuss that next time. Second, it's not exact. Einstein had a modifier. We know it isn't quite right yet because they have to put the quantum theory in. That's the same with all our other laws. They're not exact. There's always an edge of mystery. There's always a place that we have some fiddling around, do you? That, of course, is not a property, probably not a property. It may or may not be a property of nature, but it certainly is common with all the laws.
cues.zh: 第一点是它的表达是数学化的，其他定律也是如此，我们下次再探讨这一点；第二点，它并不精确，爱因斯坦曾对其进行修正，而我们知道它现在仍不完全正确，因为还必须把量子理论融入进去；我们所有其他的定律也是如此，它们都不精确，总有一丝神秘的边缘，总有一些需要我们反复修修补补的地方，不是吗？当然，这未必是大自然的属性，但也可能就是其固有属性，但它在目前已知的所有定律中确实普遍存在。

cues.en: As we know them today, it may be only a lack of knowledge. But the most impressive fact is that gravity is simple. It is simple to state the principle completely and have not left any vagueness for anybody to change the ideas about. It's simple and therefore it's beautiful. It's simple in its pattern. I don't mean it's simple in its action. The motions of the various planets and the perturbations of one another can be quite complicated to work out.
cues.zh: 这或许只是由于我们认识的局限，但最令人震撼的事实是，引力非常简单；它的原理表述起来极为简明，没有留下任何模糊空间供人随意曲解；它很纯粹，因而很美丽；它在形式结构上是简单的，但我并不是说它在具体作用上很简单，各大行星的运动以及彼此之间的摄动计算起来可能会相当复杂。

cues.en: But to follow how all those stars in the globular cluster move is quite beyond our ability. It's complicated in its actions, but not in the basic pattern or the system underneath the whole thing. That's a simple thing. That's common in all our laws. They all turn out to be simple things, although complex in their actual actions. Finally comes the universality of the gravitational law, the factor that extends over such enormous distances.
cues.zh: 要是想弄清球状星团中所有那些恒星是如何运动的，那完全超出了我们的能力；它在实际表现上很复杂，但在底层的基本模式或系统中却并非如此；那是很简单的，这也存在于我们所有的定律中，它们归根结底都很简单，尽管实际的作用过程极为复杂；最后就是引力定律的普适性，即它能延伸到如此遥远尺度的这一特性。

cues.en: that Newton, in his mind, worrying about the solar system, was able to predict what would happen in an experiment of Cavendish. Where Cavendish's little model of the solar system, the two balls attracting, has to be expanded ten million, million times to become the solar system. And then, ten million, million times expanded once again, and we find the galaxies attracting each other by exactly the same law. Nature uses only the longest threads, the weaver patterns.
cues.zh: 当年牛顿心中思索着太阳系，却能够预测出卡文迪许实验中会发生什么；在卡文迪许的小型太阳系模型里，两个小球相互吸引，而把这个尺度放大十万亿倍，才会成为真正的太阳系；然后再放大十万亿倍，我们发现星系之间也是遵循完全相同的定律相互吸引；大自然只用最长的线织出她的图案。

cues.en: so that each small piece of her fabric reveals the organization of the entire tapestry. Thank you.
cues.zh: 因此，她织物上的每一小块碎片，都能展现出整幅织锦的宏伟构造。谢谢大家。
